== Plot ==
In 1944, at the height of the Second World War, the [[Allies of World War II|Allied powers]] prepare to invade [[German-occupied Europe]] under [[Operation Overlord]]. Helmed by Gen. [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]] - the [[Supreme Allied Commander Europe]], the invasion is set to begin on 5 June ([[D-Day (military term)|D-Day]]) with multiple amphibious landings at [[Normandy landings|Normandy, France]]. Aware of invasion's enormity, and equally devastated by the failure of the pre-D-Day rehearsal [[Exercise Tiger]] six weeks earlier, he is privately wary of the operation.

On 2 June, Eisenhower summons [[Met Office]] [[meteorologist]] Gp Capt. [[James Stagg]]{{efn|In truth, Stagg was a geophysicist by training.}} to [[Southwick House]], the seat of the [[Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force]] (SHAEF) and requests him to provide a forecast favorable for Allied operations for D-Day, which is set to commence in the next 61 hours. Duly appointed as SHAEF's chief meteorological officer{{efn|Stagg joined SHAEF in November 1943, seven months before D-Day.}}, Stagg leads the British-U.S. team tasked with predicting D-Day's forecast, and is introduced to the bombastic Col. [[Irving P. Krick]], who leads the U.S. section of the team. Stagg immediately has them gather, analyze and compile [[meteorological intelligence]] collected by all weather stations within a 2,000 kilometre radius of Normandy to prepare a comprehensive forecast, and promptly predicts two [[Low-pressure area|low-pressure storms]] headed straight for the [[English Channel]] - indicating heavy rain, cloudy skies and high waves, which could render the invasion unfeasible.

Eisenhower]] - the [[Supreme Allied Commander Europe]], the invasion is set to begin on 5 June ([[D-Day (military term)|D-Day]]) with multiple amphibious landings at [[Normandy landings|Normandy, France]]. Aware of invasion's enormity, and equally devastated by the failure of the pre-D-Day rehearsal [[Exercise Tiger]] six weeks earlier, he is privately wary of the operation.

On 2 June, Eisenhower summons [[Met Office]] [[meteorologist]] Gp Capt. [[James Stagg]] to [[Southwick House]], the seat of the [[Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force]] (SHAEF) and tasks him with providing a favorable forecast for D-Day within the next 61 hours.{{efn|In truth, Stagg was a geophysicist and had joined SHAEF in November 1943, seven months before D-Day.}}
